ORGANIZATION AND ESTABLISHMENT OF PERMANENT STAFF POSITIONS-TEMPORARY EMPLOYEES PERFORMING CONTINUOUS DUTIES
speechtext: I have the honour to lay before the house the organization and establishment of the permanent positions on the staff of the House of Commons, together with a letter from the clerk of the house recommending that the temporary clerks and employees performing continuous duties be absorbed into the permanent staff of the house.

maintopic: ORGANIZATION AND ESTABLISHMENT OF PERMANENT STAFF POSITIONS-TEMPORARY EMPLOYEES PERFORMING CONTINUOUS DUTIES
speechtext:
May I ask that this report be read? I understand it is brief.
The clerk assistant read the report, as follows:
Ottawa, April 28, 1939. The Hon. Pierre F. Casgrain, K.C., M.P., Speaker of the House of Commons,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Sir:
The Commissioners of Internal Economy having approved the recommendation that all the clerks and employees of the house doing continuous work be appointed permanent, a resolution of the house must be passed creating a certain number of positions which have been filled by temporaries for a number of years. This is necessitated by the fact that the provisions of the Civil Service Act dealing with organization do not apply to our service. The act only applies to our permanent positions in relation to appointment, transfer, promotion, salaries, increases thereof, classification, political partisanship and payment of gratuity on death. It has no application with regard to our temporary staff. The volume of work necessitated by sessions of parliament having considerably increased in the last twenty years, new clerks appointed as temporary had to be kept on the staff the whole year round, but they do not have the benefit of permanency and superannuation.
As to the sergeant-at-arms' division, most of the employees are now temporary. Their services being required the whole year, it is advisable that they should become permanent.
The list hereto annexed shows the present staff, the proposed changes and the permanent positions to be created. All the new positions mentioned therein are now filled and will not necessitate new appointments. Should this reorganization be approved by the house, it will be necessary, under the provisions of the Civil Service Act, to request the Civil Service Commission to make the appointment and fix the salaries.
The committee appointed by the Senate with the same purpose in view, with whom we both had the honour of holding a conference, have agreed to submit a similar plan to the upper house and the Civil Service Commission intends to consider simultaneously the recommendations made by the two houses of parliament.
In the event of these permanencies being approved, temporary employment on our staff when parliament is not in session will be discontinued.
I have the honour to be,
Sir,
Your obedient servant,
Arthur Beauchesne,
Clerk of the House of Commons.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, April 26, consideration of the motion of Hon. Charles A. Dunning (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Budget-Mr. Lawson

ucts in a foreign market. As Canada's export trade has decreased by 15-1 per cent, there is a corresponding decrease in the national income of our people from exports. I do not suggest that any government can compel foreign countries to buy more of our goods than they desire, but I do claim the effect upon our internal economy is lessened if we develop a balanced economy for Canada. Then we are less dependent upon foreign trade for the maintenance of agricultural prices and industrial activity, and more self-reliant because of our own capacity to consume.
This political philosophy is by no means new to the people of this country. It was enunciated many years ago by the Conservative party as a national policy. It has been described recently by our Liberal friends as economic nationalism. We of the Conservative party have never advocated economic nationalism. We realize that in order to return' to the days of prosperity there must be a balanced development of world trade. But we also realize that you cannot return to a maximum development of a balanced world trade while countries with large populations are spending their energies and their efforts on the production of the materials of war. They are struggling always and constantly for the development of self-sufficiency, and the least possible dependence on other countries for goods. That is our situation to-day.
In these circumstances why does the government sit idly by, expressing pious hopes for the future, realizing, as it must, that it can do nothing to increase that world trade? Surely in these circumstances the prime motive of any government must be, necessarily, the development of consumptive power within our own country to consume our own products. And here I am not referring to the sort of consumptive power which is to be given away freely, without payment therefor in goods or services, as advocated by our social credit friends. I am speaking of an effective consumptive power. How can you create a consumptive power for agricultural products, for boots and clothing, for all the things that people need, unless you provide those people with jobs? How, I ask, can you provide those people with jobs if the result of your fiscal policy is to have greater consumption of imported goods without a corresponding increase in the export of our own domestic production? To accomplish a balanced economy is the policy of the Conservative party. You can never do it by the consummation of trade treaties, such as those which have been made by this government with the United States.

In his budget speech this year, to bolster up the efficacy of the new trade agreement entered into with the United States, the Minister of Finance was careful to point out that our exports of merchandise to that country, exclusive of gold, for the first quarter of this year, 1939, registered a gain of nearly 16 per cent over the total for the same period for 1938. What does that indicate? I hope it means a great deal more than the result of the previous trade ; greement made by this government with the United States, the agreement which came into effect on January 1, 1936. Exactly the same experience was had then as now. In the first quarter that that trade agreement was in effect our exports to the United States were increased. Then they were followed by a gradual falling off until they reached a low point in the first quarter of 1938-which quarter the minister now chooses for comparison with the first quarter of 1939.
Let me now give figures to prove my statement. The exports of Canada to the United States for the first quarter of 1935 were valued at $78,540,000. The Canada-United States trade agreement came into effect on January 1, 1936, and the exports of Canada to the United States for the first quarter of 1936 went up to $80,273,000. As the effect of the treaty gained momentum, the exports jumped, and for the first quarter of 1937 they were valued at $108,623,000. Then, as we of the Conservative party in this house predicted, there came a time when our imports constantly climbed, but our exports to the United States went down. The result was that for the first quarter of 1938 we exported to the United States goods to the value of only $61,574,000, representing a decline of about $47,000,000 from the first quarter of 1937.

speechtext: And better than last year.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Every Canadian exporter who could export his products to the United States hastened to do so as soon as the new trade treaty came into effect on January 1, 1939. Were it not for the quotas with respect to some agricultural products, limiting the quantity which may be exported to the

The Budget-Mr. Lawson
United States in any one year, there might be some chance for our maintaining our exports to that country on a level with those of the first quarter of 1939. But already many of the quotas for the whole year have been practically filled; consequently you will find a gradual diminution in the other quarters of 1939 in the volume of our exports to the United States, just as was experienced in connection with the trade agreement with the United States which came into effect on January 1, 1936.
Judging by the utterances of the Minister of Finance the government has at last come to a realization of the fact that our vital problems of taxation, unemployment and prices for agricultural products cannot be solved by the panacea of trade agreements. The minister went to some length to emphasize the necessity of the consumption of durable or capital goods in our internal economy. I would go farther than he has gone, because I am convinced that one of the major factors causing our depressed condition is the lack of consumption of durable goods. My recollection is that in a pamphlet published by one of the bureaux of research connected with the Rockefeller foundation it was stated that at the depth of the depression the falling off in the consumption and use of capital or durable goods was about sixty per cent, whereas the reduction in the consumption and use of consumable goods was only about ten per cent.
On two occasions in his address the minister, referring to bank deposits in Canada, pointed out that at the end of March, 1939, they aggregated $2,845,000,000, or 22-2 per cent above the level of March, 1938, and 8-8 per cent above the level of March in the boom year 1929. He stated further that comparing 1938 with the depression year 1932, the average volume of bank deposits in Sweden had increased by 15 per cent, in Australia by 16 per cent, in the United States by 22 per cent, in the United Kingdom by 23 per cent, and in Canada by over 25 per cent. In other words he proved that in March, 1939, we had a greater amount of money on deposit in our banks than at any other time in recent years, and that we had a greater increase, in proportion, in the volume of our bank deposits between the depth of the depression in 1932 and last March than had Sweden, Australia, the United States or the United Kingdom.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the volume of bank deposits is inextricably interwoven with the lack of consumption of durable or capital goods. When we realize that there are approximately 4,500,000 deposit accounts we must conclude that the reason for that 71492-2111
huge aggregate of bank deposits is that hundreds of people who have money to invest are not investing it in the creation of new Canadian enterprise. If that portion of those deposits which represents savings surplus, available for investment, were invested in Canadian enterprise and Canadian industry, you would immediately increase the consumption of durable goods by reason of new construction, new plants, new machinery, and that in turn would create new jobs.
Why have we this vast sum on deposit in the banks of Canada? The minister says it is because of lack of enterprise and courage on the part of the business men of Canada, and because of fear of war on the part of people who have money to invest. I will not for one moment suggest that all the business men of Canada have that vision for the future which the minister so much desires. I will not suggest that all business men in Canada have put forth their utmost effort for the development of new enterprise and new industry. But I do suggest that if this government will enunciate such fiscal policies as will give reasonable security for the investment of that capital in Canadian enterprise and Canadian industry, you will get results.
I should like to point out to the government that in these modern days industry is not organized on the basis of twenty or twenty-five years ago. The individual industrialists left in this country are few and far between. Canadian enterprise and Canadian industry are in large measure carried on in these modern days by corporations which are aggregates of large numbers of small investors or combinations or groups of business men. No matter how much courage or enterprise business men may have, they cannot embark upon new enterprise and new industry unless they can induce a vast number of the people who have savings, to invest their savings in new industries. Unless you give them a measure of security

some assurance that over a reasonable period of years they will be given an opportunity to compete in their own domestic market in the sale of the product produced by such industry at a price which will return a reasonable reward upon the investment made -they will not invest their savings.
To-day there is no such security. Every year since this government has been in power there has been constant tinkering with the tariff, either because of trade agreements or because of reductions contained in budget proposals. I do not suggest for one moment that we should have no change in our tariff. I do not suggest for one moment that in the past we have not had tariffs, in respect of some particular industries, the result of which
The Budget-Mr. Lawson

was to create a virtual monopoly in the Canadian market and thus penalize the consumer in the matter of price. But I still say that in order to induce business men to create new industries we must have stability of tariff. I repeat what I said on Tuesday last, speaking in this house, that when we created the tariff board I had hopes that if that tariff board were allowed to function free from political influence we would begin to have a scientific tariff-a truly protective but not monopolistic tariff-after the expiration of ten years. I still hold that hope. Now that this government has glutted itself with trade agreements, why not try stability of tariff as a means of creating new industries, greater consumption of capital goods, more jobs for the unemployed, and, resulting therefrom, greater consumption and better prices for our agricultural products?
Can it be done without penalizing the consumer?	I believe it can. We have
this quasi-judicial, non-political tariff board. Why not use it?	If this government
were to adopt a policy which would clearly indicate to business men and to those who have capital to invest that for the period of the next five years there would be no reduction in the tariff of this country, where such reduction would affect established Canadian industries, except as a result of a recommendation by the tariff board after due inquiry by the board, I will guarantee that that would do more to create new enterprise and industry, to cause the investment of accumulated capital in the production of goods, and to create jobs and payrolls, than would any measure for the reduction of income tax, such as is proposed in this budget. Let us have stability of tariff and security for industry and I venture to predict that you will soon be on the high road to prosperity.
The minister stated that foreign investors had convincingly demonstrated their faith in this country's future by investing their capital in Canadian enterprise. I fear he is all too altruistic if he concludes that that is done because of any opportunities afforded by any legislation of this government. Any capital invested by foreign investors in this country within the last few years has been so invested for only one of two reasons-either because it was driven from the country *whence it came by tax laws and restrictions which amounted to expropriation, or because a more profitable return could be assured from investment in Canada. It will fly from Canada to some other place as soon as a greater opportunity is available.
Now let the minister smile at this next statement. Into w'hat type of investment has

that foreign capital been put? Into Canadian government bonds, into Canadian National railway bonds guaranteed by the government, and into mining securities. Such capital has no fixed place of abode. It has no patriotism. Foreign capital is an asset to this or any other country only to the extent to which it provides the necessary capital for the development of domestic enterprises, where such domestic enterprise results from the development of natural resources, when domestic capital is not available. Canada will get more permanent benefit from the investment of one Canadian investor's dollar in industry than it will from every ten dollars of foreign capital invested in government bonds.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will my hon. friend permit i question? I hesitate to interrupt him.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He has asked for a specific statement. I can make the specific statement that the situation to which I referred in the budget was definitely contemplated at the time the treaty was made. The extent to which we would subsequently remove the excise tax was left for further determination, but certainly the whole question was envisaged, necessarily. I am not taking any credit for it, because one could not miss it; it stuck out plainly as something that had to be dealt with. I might point out to my hon. friend a slight error on his part, namely, that under the proposals the excise will still apply under the general tariff. To that extent he is in error.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, it will apply under the general tariff. But in view of the fact that this government boasts of the trade agreements it has made with all countries, in view of the fact that as a result of the Canada-United States trade agreement the most favoured nation clause applies to all our trade treaties, practically the vast bulk of the imports of the country come in under the intermediate tariff, and therefore what my hon. friend says does not apply.
Now let me accept the minister's statement. I find it difficult to conceive that this government, for the purpose of making a trade agreement with the United States, would pay the price which they must have realized they would have to pay by a complete repeal of the three per cent excise tax, which was in the nature of a tariff. I simply cannot conceive that this government would take that action in the interests of this country.
The minister further said:
I am sure that the action I am proposing today-
That is, repealing the excise tax.
-which will involve an estimated reduction in taxation of about $14,000,000, will commend itself to all interests in this country, whether manufacturers, importers or consumers.
[Mr. Lawson.}
I can readily appreciate that the repeal of the excise tax would commend itself to importers; but for the life of me I am unable to appreciate why it should commend itself to manufacturers or to consumers who represent the wage-earning class in this country. The excise tax added nothing to the price of goods manufactured in Canada.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about automobiles?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Huron North (Mr. Deachman) says no. My answer is no. As I previously stated, the excise tax was not a tax in the true sense of the word. It amounted, in truth and in fact, to a protective tariff against the imports of foreign goods. Nothing more clearly proves my point than the glaring example of what would have happened by reason of the repeal of that tax, an example so glaring that even this government, dull of perception, realized the effect it would have with respect to the imports of crude rubber and primary forms of tin. Consequently in this budget they substituted for the excise tax a duty of five per cent ad valorem on such goods.
To illustrate the effect of taking off the excise tax without imposing some corresponding ad valorem tariff, I am going to take two examples. First, let me illustrate the effect the removal would have had on the importations of crude rubber had a new tariff not been substituted therefor. The excise tax was first introduced in Canada on June 2,
1931,	to the extent of one per cent on importations, with a restricted free list. On April 7,
1932,	at the time of the empire trade agreements it was increased to three per cent. In 1933 the total amount of imports of crude rubber into this country was 728 carloads of
60,000	pounds each. Of that importation of 728 carloads, only four carloads entered Canada through Canadian ports. In 1935 the three per cent excise tax in respect of imports under the British preferential tariff was entirely repealed by the former Conservative government. Note what happened in respect of imports of crude rubber during the years 1936, 1937 and 1938; eighty-four per cent of all the imports of crude rubber into this country during those years entered through Canadian ports. Why? Because of the application of the three per cent excise tax if they had entered through United States ports. The result was that Canadian ports got the business of handling that importation. Rubber was hauled by Canadian railroads. The financial business in connection with the

The Budget-Mr. Lawson
payment for the shipments was handled by Canadian banks. Canadian harbour boards got revenues from storage, wharfage, and so forth. Canadian stevedores, longshoremen and labourers got work. The railways of Canada derived revenues from the hauling of crude rubber, thus providing employment for Canadian railway workers. Were it not for the special five per cent ad valorem tax proposed by this budget to replace the three per cent excise tax repealed in respect of crude rubber, all that business would go back to the United States ports. As there are no increases in tariff generally provided in the budget to offset the repeal of the three per cent excise tax, many other products will share a similar fate to that which would have resulted in the case of the importation of crude rubber.
Let me take another example. I choose the automobile industry, because it has been successively before the tariff board for three years; hence official data and statistics are available in connection therewith.
By the Canada-United States trade agreement of 1935 the intermediate tariff became applicable to automobiles and automobile parts entering Canada, resulting in a tariff on automobiles of 17-| per cent. The whole question of the tariff on automobiles and parts was referred to the tariff board, which conducted a most exhaustive investigation and made a report on April 27, 1936. In its report the tariff board recommended that the intermediate tariff imposed on imported automobiles should remain temporarily at 17J per cent. The tariff board however realized that it was quite possible that the automobile industry would not be continued in Canada under a 17^ per cent tariff, and therefore recommended that the government should take power by order in council to increase that intermediate tariff to 22i per cent should it be found that any motor car manufacturer ceased to manufacture in Canada. I quote from the report of the tariff board of April 27, 1936:
With respect to the suggested tariff item 438a, the board is of the opinion that under present conditions and after giving effect to the changes contained in the above schedule, the rates set opposite the above suggested item are sufficiently adequate to protect the industry in Canada.
Item 438a was the automobile tariff item, and the schedule referred to was the recommendation for an intermediate tariff of 17-J per cent. I continue the quotation:
If, for some reason or other, one of the manufacturers presently in operation in Canada should discontinue production, a situation might well be created whereby the position of the remaining ear manufacturers might be jeopardized. So as to provide for such an eventuality the board is of the opinion that the governor in council should be empowered to increase the rates to the extent indicated in the proviso-
That is, 22J per cent.

if in the judgment of the governor in council the situation created warrants such action.
The very same report recommended that a special excise tax of five per cent should be imposed on that portion of the dealer's price of automobiles which is in excess of $650, ivith a maximum levy on each vehicle not in excess of $250, in addition to the three per cent excise already in effect.
Subsequent to that recommendation of the tariff board the Studebaker corporation withdrew from manufacturing automobiles in Canada. IIudson-Essex continued to make a few cars in Canada, but tremendously curtailed its manufacturing operations. Despite the recommendation of the tariff board and the withdrawal of Studebaker and Hudson-Essex, not one thing was done by this government to meet the situation.
What was the result of the government's failure to act? In 1936 the total number of motor vehicles imported into Canada was 8,053. In 1937 imports jumped to 17,267. The number of motor trucks imported into Canada in 1936 was 1,850, but in 1937 the imports jumped to 2,808. Adding those figures together it will be seen that the total number of motor units imported into Canada in 1936 was 9,903 and in 1937 the total was 20,075. That is, there were 10,172 more motor units imported into Canada in 1937 than in 1936, or an increase in imports of approximately fifty per cent.
It will be observed that the tariff board recommended a special excise tax of five per cent on the top portion of the dealer's price, as well as the three per cent excise tax. The tariff board was of the opinion that this was a minimum protective tariff under which the motor car industry could subsist; yet by this budget it is proposed to repeal the three per cent excise, the result of which is further to reduce the tariff in respect of the automobile industry.
Is this industry worth while to Canada? Ever since I have been in this house I have heard this question bandied back and forth across the floor. Allegations were made pro and con without any findings of fact by an independent tribunal to back up the assertions. Now we have the advantage of the tariff board reports with respect to this industry, and their conclusions after weeks and months of investigation. Despite the fifty per cent increase in importations of motor units into Canada in 1937 over 1936 which I have detailed, the average monthly employ-. ment given by the automobile industry in Canada during 1937 was 31,494 and the wages paid during 1937 amounted to $43,069,973.
The Budget-Mr. Lawson

That indicates that the automobile industry-provided 31,494 jobs at an average wage of slightly less than $1,400 per annum.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: At what cost to the consumers of Canada?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am coming to that. If my hon. friend will hold himself in peace he will learn that always when I have a statement to make I finish it before I leave it.
Is not that industry worth while? There are those who say that the consumer pays too high a price for the benefit of jobs for those employed in the motor car industry. Well, the tariff board dealt with that. I quote from their report of 1936. In the summary they say:
In section A of chapter 8 of this report the board has listed certain factors that might have to be weighed before arriving at an appraisal of the economic value of the automotive industry in Canada. The figures given therein would indicate that the increase in the total amount paid by dealers in Canada for automobiles and trucks and replacement parts thereof, in 1934, to the Canadian automotive industry, in excess of the amount that they would have paid if automobiles were permitted free entry into Canada, not including freight or licences, is approximately $14,000,000. As against this amount the board has also listed in that section of the report the disbursements that were made in 1934 in Canada for taxes-federal, provincial and municipal-for freight to transportation systems, for wages and salaries and for expense, materials and service, which are directly attributable to the existence of the automotive industry in Canada. These disbursements were from $40,000,000 to $47,000,000.
The board, while not accepting the above comparison as an accurate measure of the value of the industry to Canada, is of the opinion, nevertheless, that the figures would indicate that it is good business for Canada reasonably to encourage the maintenance and the expansion of the Canadian automotive industry.
I think that is an answer to my hon. friend's question. I have heard the statement made that the repeal of the excise tax will wipe out the motor car industry in this country. I heard the Minister of Finance strenuously deny that statement and declare that the motor industry would carry on. In a measure I agree with the Minister of Finance. The primary automobile industries in Canada, those that make the cars as distinct from those that make parts for the makers of the cars, are in all cases subsidiaries of United States corporations. The only factor that determines whether or not they will manufacture cars in Canada is whether it is more economical for them to manufacture here than in the United States. Their natural inclination would be to manufacture in the United States. By reason of the fiscal policy of past Conservative governments these corporations were com-

pelled to establish plants in Canada in order to supply the Canadian market, thereby providing jobs in Canadian factories and payrolls for Canadian workers. The fiscal policies of former Conservative governments made it advantageous for the motor car companies to manufacture cars in Canada for export to other parts of the British empire, because of preferential rates of duty which they obtained for Canadian made cars in empire markets.
The United States motor car industry has a large investment in plant and machinery in Canada. It will continue to manufacture in Canada a certain number of motor cars for export and probably some proportion of cars for domestic sale, because of the preferential advantage that still obtains in empire markets and because it does not wish to have lying idle, plant and equipment in which it has invested many thousands of dollars. The fact remains, however, that as a result of the repeal of this three per cent excise tax the number of motor units manufactured in Canada will be tremendously reduced, thus causing further unemployment not only in the plants that manufacture the cars but also in the plants that manufacture parts for the motor cars, which parts industry is scattered widely throughout a large portion of the province of Ontario and in a considerable number of places in the province of Quebec. I cannot conceive of any reason for the failure on the part of this government to increase the automobile tariff by five per cent, as originally recommended by the tariff board, particularly now as a substitute for the three per cent excise tax which is being repealed, except to appease the clamour of the government's Liberal supporters in this house who come from western Canada.
The conditions I have illustrated by an analysis of the situation in connection with the motor car industry will apply to many other industries in this country. I predict that the removal of the three per cent excise tax without any corresponding increase in protective tariff against the imports from nearly all the other countries of the world will create further unemployment in and occasion further loss to the Canadian economy.
Now let us consider the financial aspect of this budget. The funded debt of Canada on March 31, 1939, is shown by the minister to have been $3,318,479,000. The funded debt of Canada as of March 31, 1938, the end of the previous fiscal year, was $3,252,587,000. therefore there has been an increase in the funded debt during the past year of $55,-
892,000.	The minister estimates an over-all deficit for the year just ended of $55,666,000. If you add that amount to the increase in the

The Budget-Mr. Lawson
funded debt during the last fiscal year, you get a total increase in our debt amounting to
8111,558,000.	In arriving at that deficit for the past year, however, the minister estimated a loss of only $25,000,000 in respect of the 1938 wheat crop. Previously this session, if my recollection serves me aright, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) stated that the loss in respect of the 1938 wheat crop would amout to $48,000,000. If the figure given by the Minister of Agriculture is correct we must add another $23,000,000 in order to determine the total increase in the debt of this country under the administration of the present government during the fiscal year ended March 31, 1939. If you add that $23,000,000 you get a figure of $134,558,000. Therefore, despite the fact that $20,000,000 less was spent by this government for the relief of unemployment and agricultural distress in the past fiscal year as compared with the previous year, during next year Canada will have to pay interest upon an additional sum of $134,558,000, and that interest can come only from one source; that is, out of the pockets of the people in the form of taxes. That is the picture resulting from the government's management of the business of this country for the past year.
In speaking on the budget last year I made the statement that this government possessed the doubtful honour of being the greatest tax collector in the history of Canada. This year they have collected from the people in taxes an amount less by $13,000,000 than they collected in the preceding year; nevertheless they still hold the record as the greatest tax collectors in the history of Canada. For the fiscal year ended March 31, 1936, the total amount of taxes collected from the people was $317,312,000. The Liberal government came into power in 1935, so that they have been entirely responsible for any increase in taxation, or for the collection of any increased amount of taxes from the people, since that date. Last year they collected in taxes $435,-
705,000,	or $118,393,000 more than was collected during the last fiscal year in which the Conservative government was in power.
Let us look at their expenditures. I shall not refer to the total expenditures, because that would include unemployment relief, grants in aid to the provinces, the dominion's share of joint dominion-provincial projects, the western drought area relief, bonus to wheat growers, and so on. I shall deal with the total ordinary expenditures, namely those which are under direct control of the government, and which are not affected by special expenditures to meet distress, deprivation or want.
In the last year in which the Conservative administration controlled expenditures, namely
the year ended March 31, 1936, the total controllable expenditure was 8372,539,000. In the year ended March 31, 1939, the minister himself gives as his estimate of the controllable expenditures the sum of $416,372,000. In other words, in the last fiscal year the government spent $43,833,000 more than was spent by the Conservative administration in the last year in which its policies could have any effect upon the controllable expenditures of this country. Comparing the fiscal year ended March 31, 1939, with the previous fiscal year ended March 31, 1938, we have an increase in controllable expenditures of SI ,500,000 and a decrease in revenue from taxation of about $13,000,000. The revenues are down, but controllable expenditures are up-attributable not to the fixed price of wheat, not to the relief of unemployment, because those figures are not included in the figures I have given, but to a weak and wasteful administration.
Where did some of that money go? Well, $1,453,903.89 was spent on commissions authorized by this government to do jobs which in the main are the responsibility of the government, as the elected representatives of the people. Where did some more of that increase in expenditures go to?-increased civil service staff. At the end of March 1936 we had a total of 41,132 permanent and temporary employees in our dominion civil service. That figue is official. No figures are available at all as of March 31, 1939. Official figures are not even yet available for the year ended March 31, 1938. But I am credibly informed that an accurate estimate for the end of March 1938 would be 44,102. If that estimate is correct, then during the two years 1937 and 1938, under the administration of this government, the number of civil servants was increased by 2,970. I will guarantee that when the figures for March 31, 1939, are available we shall find that there is again a further increase in the number of civil servants employed by the federal government. Why is it necessary for this government to employ 3,000 more civil servants than were employed in 1935 by the Conservative government?
That is the record of last year. To what may we look forward in the next year? The prospects for the coming year are further deficits and further debt upon the people. The .minister states the total expenditures for the year ending March 31, 1940, leaving aside $29,400,000 of capital expenditures for defence-which will have to be added to our present debt-will amount to $550,100,000. He then proceeds to estimate that the revenue will equal $490,000,000. How on earth he arrives at that figure is difficult to determine.
The Budget

Mr. Lawson

In the year just closed the total revenue was $501,677,000. No increases in taxation are proposed in this budget. On the contrary we are going to lose at least $14,000,000 in revenue from excise tax. If the proposed reduction in the income tax of corporations accomplishes the purpose for which it is intended we will lose another $10,000,000 in income tax. If we take these losses of revenue, amounting to $24,000,000, and deduct that amount from the $501,000,000 collected last year, it leaves the minister with a maximum gross revenue of $477,000,000, plus a hope that changed world conditions will drift this drifting government into a tide of improved business conditions, and hence larger income.
However, on the basis of the estimate given by the minister we face the prospect of a deficit of $60,000,000 in the coming year. This does not take into account any loss in excess of $25,000,000 in respect of the wheat crop of 1938, or any loss on the wheat crop of 1939 by reason of the minimum guaranteed price per bushel or the bonus per acre. Nor does it take into account the $29,400,000 of capital expenditures for defence purposes. So that in the result I venture to predict that there will be a deficit of not $60,000,000 but close to $90,000,000 on current account, unless revenues tremendously improve. There will be a capital expenditure of $29,400,000 to be added to the burden of debt upon the people for deficit in current account, making a total increase in debt of approximately $120,000,000.
Is no vigorous, courageous policy to be announced by the government to meet this appalling situation? I agree with the Minister of Finance that we should not embark upon a policy of pump priming. I do not believe that will ever solve our problem. I agree with him that the mere fact of an unbalanced budget is not in itself injurious to general economic welfare. I agree that the government should not embark upon a policy of deflation, because to do so would only impose a further burden upon those who are least able to bear it. I do say that this government should adopt a vigorous, definite and determined policy to reduce that deficit by reducing controllable expenditures, instead of merely drifting with the tide of political expediency.
You will never reduce controllable expenditures by constantly increasing the number of civil servants. You will never reduce controllable expenditures by putting enactments on our statute books such as that sponsored by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Fuler) this session to set up a motion picture bureau, entailing a commissioner and the staff which the commissioner will require. You

will attain it only by the government giving virile, strong leadership to business and enterprise and to the people of this country. The Minister of Finance "passes the buck" for leadership to the business men of this country. The minister said:
It is in the field of private investment that leadership and courage are most needed to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I hope my hon. friend will read what preceded that, because I had no intention of "passing the buck." I was acknowledging the deficiencies both of my hon. friends and of myself.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I quite admit the Minister of Finance intended to put it in that way. I have not the quotation before me, but his words were to the effect that he was not placing greater blame on the business men than upon himself. I think that is a fair interpretation of his remarks. The minister says he was not "passing the buck," but in my opinion he was "passing the buck" to the business men on behalf of the government. I cannot agree with that statement. I do agree that the government requires the cooperation of private investment and of the business men of Canada to attain the solution of our problems, but the business men and the private investors were not the ones chosen by the people to give leadership. The people chose this government. If you want to get cooperation and activity from private investors and from the business men of this country, the government must lead. I am confident that business will follow. I am sure that if the government will come forward with a policy which has the qualities the minister so much desires in business, of leadership and courage; if it will attempt an administration that seriously seeks to curtail controllable expenditure instead of being blown 'by every wind of political expediency, the government will have the cooperation of private investors and the business men of this country irrespective of their political faith.
We have heard a great deal recently of the leadership league. Why was it created? It is but an expression of the demand of the people for that leadership which the government of the day should give and which this government promised when they obtained the votes of the people in 1935. The reason you have so much talk about leadership and leadership leagues to-day is that the public are becoming tax conscious and are realizing as never before the part that government plays in increasing or lessening their burdens. Last year the people of this country were called upon to provide in excess of $54,000,000 to pay the deficit on the people's railroad. What

The Budget-Mr. Coldwell
leadership has been given by the government to cut down that deficit and solve 'that railway problem? The only leadership I have been able to observe is that two ministers of the crown were the first to announce an expenditure on the part of that railway of 812,500,000 to build a new railway station in the city of Montreal.

speechtext: During the by-election.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Do not get ahead of me. The only leadership given there was to lead into a further deficit of 812,500,000 so that the Liberal candidate would lead all the other candidates in a by-election then pending in the territory immediately benefited by the expenditure. What leadership has the government given to effect savings in connection with the operation of the Canadian National Railways? Up to the present time the only contribution made to savings on that railway has been the minute amounts saved by reducing the number of sectionmen employed, or the trainmen and brakemen running on the line, instead of using a pruning knife effectively to eliminate the extravagant expenditure at the top for private cars and high-salaried executives who are failing in their primary jab of reducing the cost of the operation of the railway.
I repeat, the people of this country are becoming tax conscious. Almost every revolt in every country in the history of this world has had its origin in tax consciousness of the people, consequent upon tax oppression. The never-ending and ever-increasing expenditure of this government is driving the people to revolt, but, being Canadians, they are expressing their revulsion against this government for its do-nothing, drifting policy in the form of leadership leagues, tax repeal associations and committees for railway action. They are expressing their revulsion against this government for its increase of the public debt, for its lack of progressive policies, for its lack of leadership.
I therefore move:
That all the words after "that" in the said motion be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"This house regrets that, in violation of its pledges to the electors, the government does not propose to lighten by reduction of controllable expenditure the heaviest taxation ever imposed on the Canadian people, taxation that retards exchange of goods and expansion of industry, discourages investment of capital in new enterprises, and perpetuates the major problem of unemployment;
That the government has failed to adopt measures for the preservation of domestic markets for the products "f the farm and fisheries*
That no adequate solution has been offered by the government of vital pressing problems relating to youth, work and wages for willing hands and cooperation with the provinces towards national understanding and the common good."

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first word is one of congratulation to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) upon his very apparent improvement in health. I am sure we are all glad to see him able to perform the most arduous duty of introducing a budget and making a budget speech. I should like to do what I have done before, congratulate him upon the manner in which that speech was presented and the clarity of expression which, as usual, characterized it. I liked the new method of introducing the budget by which the various schedules eliminate from the speech a great deal of detail. Having said this, I am bound to say that considered from the point of view of the masses of the Canadian people the budget is a dismal document. It reflects an utter bankruptcy of the government and its policies in relation to the pressing problems confronting the country.
In this, the fourth budget delivered in the fourth session of this parliament, we see very very little indication-I was going to say no indication-that the government intends to fulfil many of the promises made to the Canadian people immediately prior to the general election of 1935. I have before me, for example, a report of the radio broadcasts delivered by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) immediately before the general elections of 1935, and they make interesting reading now. Almost every word he uttered then in condemnation of the preceding government can be applied with equal or even greater force to his own present administration. He says on page 4, for example:
You have had one experience of being deceived by promises at general elections. Are you prepared to risk another? You have seen how long a period of time five years is; what opportunity it affords a ministry, if the ministry be so inclined, altogether to ignore, and even to defy, your clearly expressed will and your most evident wishes.
When I think of the numerous promises made by the present Prime Minister, by the official Liberal party and by members of the Liberal party, prior to the 1935 campaign, the force of the Prime Minister's preelection warning is driven home to me at least. Where in this fourth and perhaps preelection budget is the fulfilment of the promise, for example, to use currency and credit in terms of public need? Where the promise to establish an investment control board to prevent the

The Budget-Mr, Coldwell
exploitation of the public through the sale of watered stock and worthless securities? Where the promise to bring about more democracy in industry so that workers and consumers might have a larger share in the government of industry? Where the promises to lower the costs of production in agriculture by forcing a reduction in farm implement prices? What has become of the threats of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), made immediately prior to the Saskatchewan general provincial elections, and made so eloquently in this house before those elections last June? Where is the dollar wheat promised to our western farmers so that they might meet their obligations and buy clothing for their families? All we have is several bills on the order paper foreshadowing 37-cent wheat on the farm- and ruination for western agriculture. Where is the Prime Minister's own promise to reduce the sales tax from where it then stood at six per cent? So far from reducing the sales tax the first budget introduced by the present government raised it from six to eight per cent, and there it still remains.
Where are the caustic criticisms of the sugar tax and of the other nuisance taxes against which members opposite declaimed so long and so loudly in the years before 1935? I had occasion a day or two ago to look up some of the old Hansards and I read the caustic criticisms of all these taxes made not only by gentlemen now comprising the government party but by members of the government itself. What has the government done to mitigate Canada's unemployment problem, which they described in 1935 as our most pressing national problem? In his radio address of August 5, 1935, the Prime Minister said, and again I quote from page 42 of this booklet, Mackenzie King to the Canadian People, 1935:
Taking the latest figures on employment supplied by the bureau of statistics, it can be shown that, on the most conservative estimate, there are to-day over 400,000 wage earners out of work.
The same government bureau of statistics estimates that in February, 1939, the latest report that has come to my hand, there were over 491,000 wage earners out of work, to which must be added, because in 1935 they were considered as unemployed, the 26,000 young persons employed under our farm placement plan and all other young people employed under forestry and other schemes. Referring to these unemployed and to others on relief in 1935 the present Prime Minister said, and again I quote from his radio addresses:
It is not with statistics, but with human lives, that we are concerned. You cannot measure fear, privation and want by any yardstick, or
fMr. Coldwell.]
adding machine. Who will venture to estimate what the enforced idleness of hundreds of thousands of human beings, and the enforced acceptance of relief from the state by a very much larger number, over a period of two, three, four and, for some, five years, has meant in the waJ .Physical suffering, of mental anxiety, and of human anguish to lives and homes of which there is no record whatever? Who will venture to estimate what the effect of all this may be upon the health and morale of the nation? Is it any wonder that to-day there is widespread unrest and discontent throughout l.? i*i ** ana that, in the case of young and old alike, many are in a condition of despair.
Thus eloquently the Prime Minister put the case in August, 1935. The Canadian people listened to his siren call, and to-day instead of two, three or four years of unemployment and relief these people have had six, seven and nine years of unemployment and relief.
To solve the problems of unemployment and of agriculture the Prime Minister, and again I use his own words, appealed for stability and an unmistakable majority." He got the majority and the Canadian people got the stability.
Contrast this record and this budget with those of another dominion government, elected also in 1935 to give effect to policies such as those .which the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation has consistently advocated-the Dominion of New Zealand. There they have ended unemployment and are actually busily engaged at the present time in recruiting certain classes of labour, particularly in the building trades, carpenters, for example, in the commonwealth of Australia because in New Zealand there is a shortage of such labour. We have heard Jeremiahs predict that New Zealand will shortly meet with economic difficulties. The regiments of reaction are organizing to destroy that government, and there is a consistent propaganda against it all across the world; but if they are destroyed for the time being, New Zealand will at least have had years of respite and its people will be better housed, better equipped, and with a better morale to grapple with any situation that may arise.
Here in this dominion, with the government facing failure all across the country, every attempt is now being made to end this session with our problems unsolved. We are told that if we do not agree to prorogue shortly we shall be forced to come back and sit here again in the heat of an Ottawa summer. Many of us have had a strenuous session; for we have tried to force the government to pay some heed at least to the problems to which I have referred. In my opinion parliament should adjourn for a few days to do proper homage to their majesties, but the king's business should thereafter proceed and

The Budget-Mr. Caldwell
be properly concluded. Mussolini and Hitler move into other lands to divert attention from internal difficulties. It seems to me that the Prime Minister is proposing to close parliament and tour this country and the United States as the north American adviser to his majesty, and I am persuaded that if his majesty knew the condition of his people on the farms and throughout this country generally he at least would wish that the Prime Minister and members of parliament should remain here to do their duty. For in Canada the dangers to democracy and to the throne-because the throne in this country rests upon the will of a democratic people-are to be found in the conditions within the country rather than in threats from without.
The budget, I repeat, is a dismal document. It is not a people's budget, it is a rich man's budget. There is no lowering of the sales tax, no lowering of the sugar tax, no measure of relief from taxes that strike the very poor. For the last year, according to the budget, the estimated yield from sales tax will be
8119,460,000,	or 23-81 per cent of our total revenue; from tariff and customs duties we derived S78,750,000, or 15-7 per cent of our revenue; and from excise tax, in which there is some reduction, 851,313,000 or 10-23 per cent. These I submit are taxes that are passed on in the main to the consumer, so that 49-74 per cent of our revenue last year was collected in burdens that bear heavily upon the consumers and upon their purchasing power. From this there will be some relief, but relatively little, and much of this little may not be passed on to the consumers by the monopolistic industries and distributive agencies.
Income tax accounts for some 28-31 per cent of our entire revenue. This is collected, according to the figures submitted to this house during the discussion of the estimates of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ilsley) largely from a few wealthy individuals and corporations. The budget speech proposes indirect reduction of certain corporation taxes. Already the powerful and rich mining industry enjoys rebates on account of capital invested in new projects, and now the government proposes to extend this principle to industry generally. The minister in his speech said:
Any firm, therefore, which begins after May 1 next the construction, installation, betterment, replacement or extension of plant, machinery, or fixed equipment will be allowed a credit against income tax equal to ten per cent of the costs incurred for such capital projects prior to April 30, 1940-one year.
Hence in an indirect way the corporation income tax, and individual income tax in some cases as well, is being reduced. There
is no relief from sales tax or sugar tax, no substantial relief from the burdens of tariff taxation on the clothing of the people, but substantial relief, I take it, is being given to the textile and other industries that care to take advantage of this particular provision.
This, it will be argued, will create new employment. But will it? Obsolete plants will be reconditioned and rationalized so that perhaps the ultimate result may well be more, not less unemployment. Such is the price of progress and the dilemma in which modern capitalism finds itself. Besides, what are the requirements of modern industry in Canada? Already it is said that we are over-equipped, so that even in good times industry operates only to a fraction of its potentialities. This was demonstrated again and again before the price spreads and mass buying committee some years ago. Two years ago the government raised the tariff to protect the furniture industry-why? Well, because we had too many factories, too much competition, too little rationalization and high domestic prices -again, the dilemma of unplanned, unintelligent economy. Now it is proposed to bonus all industries so that they may expand their plants and become more efficient in order to make more goods. But what we need is greater consumption of the goods we already have and greater use of the potentialities which we already possess in the country in which we live. We lower income tax on the manufacturer but we take from the consumers, by the sales tax, the tariff and the excise, about $250,000,000 worth of purchasing power. Surely the minister is beginning at the wrong end. The corporation income tax is the last, not the first tax that ought to be lowered by a government which said that personality was more sacred than property.

speechtext: The Prime Minister, before the election of course. Through the years many of these industries have taken a heavy toll in profits from the people, and now they are the first to get relief from taxation. speechtext:
Then why not 80-cent wheat?
The Budget-Mr. Coldwell

speechtext: Yes, why not 80-cent wheat? I remember hearing the leader of the opposition say on one occasion in this chamber, in relation to that increase, that since it was a creation of the government of Canada and therefore of the people, the difference ought to belong to the government and the people. In other words, when the government creates an artificial value more than commensurate to meet the needs of the industry, the government ought to consider that a national asset and use it as such.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Would the hon. member
permit a question now, or would he prefer that I wait until he is finished?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would rather the hon. member would wait, but I do not mind answering a question.
Somewhere we have to find more revenue; for I am not one of those who believe that we can tell the Canadian people now or during an election that any government elected to office can reduce taxes in the bulk.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt, but I was reading and only partly listening. I heard the hon. member say that the leader of the opposition had said that the mining industry belonged to the people, as I understood. I should like him to clarify that. I think it was to my predecessor that he referred.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, I apologize-I was referring to what the former leader of the opposition, Mr. Bennett, said concerning gold.
I was saying that if any of us tell the people of Canada that, under the conditions that exist or are likely to exist, taxation in the bulk can be reduced, we shall be misleading the people. The obligations that are going to confront Canada will require more, not less revenue. I use the term "taxation" as synonymous with "revenue" at the moment. And in my opinion these revenues must come from corporations and persons who possess great wealth, making their ability to pay equally great. To continue a sales tax of eight per cent and give rebates to industries and corporations is, in my opinion, the very antithesis of democratic financial policy.
The effect of this rebate was shown in the budget forecast presented by the Minister of Finance last Tuesday. The minister indicated anticipated receipts from income tax to be slightly less this coming year-not as much less as the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lawson) indicated, but I am inclined to agree with the hon. member for York South in his estimate. The Minister of Finance estimated that the revenue from sales tax would be more than it was in the last fiscal year. That estimate may not be borne out by experience,

but the point I make is that the minister anticipates that receipts from income tax will be less and receipts from sales tax will be more. To my mind this,"from the point of view of the Canadian people, is a wrong policy. If we are to lighten the burden of taxation anywhere it should be upon the masses of the people and not upon the corporations.
What will this concession mean? I have in my hand a copy of a reprint from the Canadian Journal of Economics and Political Science, volume 5, No. 1, February, 1939, in which this matter of replacement rebate is discussed. I quote the comment made on the final report of the national employment commission on employment conditions in Canadian industry:
The suggestion is made in the final report that special income tax allowances might be made for expenditures undertaken in order to replace obsolete industrial equipment. Can a quantitative idea be obtained of how much this is necessary? Of the firms who were circularized on the modernization or obsolescence of their plant since 1929 the percentage who reported their plants were not up to date was 21-6, and only 16-2 per cent stated further expenditures were required (19-4 per cent did not reply). The 2,742 concerns who reported their specific expenditures spent the formidable sum of $294,260,000. The 1,254 among these stating themselves to be in need of plant reequipment actually spent $44,930,000 but placed their requirements at a further $78,646,000. This is a substantial amount, all or part of which might have gone to bolster demand in the capital goods industry if tax allowances had been made. However, this must be kept in relation to the record of as much as $250,000,000 spent by firms who according to their own statement remained up to date without benefit of tax remission. These are not complete figures, of course, and a number of other points arise which cannot be pursued, but there is perhaps enough here to counsel a less unqualified approval of the proposal than it might at first evoke. How much loss of tax revenue on expenditures that did not need a stimulus is to be set against the advantage of increased expenditures made by concerns wild do?
In other words the writer of this article states that in any event from the point of view of industry the suggestion is of doubtful value, reducing the revenue to the government and at the same time perhaps giving a stimulus to industries that do not require and ought not to receive such a stimulus. In my opinion the provision may be taken advantage of by the "lame ducks" of industry as well as by powerful corporations which do not need the assistance.
I now wish to move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), an amendment to the amendment, as follows:
That the amendment be further amended by adding the following words thereto:

The Budget-Mr. Coldwell
"This house deplores the failure of the government to reduce or abolish the sales tax of eight per cent which reduces consumers' purchasing power while at the same time proposing to allow a reduction by way of a credit against income tax of ten per cent of certain capital outlays by any firm which conforms to the stipulated requirements."
That amendment really summarizes what I have been trying to say this afternoon in criticism of the budget. In my opinion these are the two features which ought to be placed in bold relief one against the other- the failure to relieve taxation on the great masses of the people, and at the same time the reduction of taxation upon industry and corporations.
We in this group are not enemies of industry. We believe industry is essential to our national life. We would do all we could to encourage industry, in the proper perspective, but what we are endeavouring to do is show that this government at least is beginning in the wrong place and in that respect doing the wrong thing. I know that those who support the government may be said at this time to be a rather strange family. I .am well aware of the political necessity for the introduction in this house at this time of a budget such as we have before us, a stand-pat budget which really makes no fundamental changes in things as they are. I have before me the Prime Minister's radio addresses. I need not quote them, but I remember how in the addresses he urged the Canadian people to return the Liberal party to power because then, he said, we would have a real national government, a really happy family of provincial and dominion premiers all across the country.

The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) says, "springtime hallucinations." I am glad he recognizes that at least some members on his own side are suffering from springtime hallucinations. I am quite sure they have been so afflicted for a considerable time.
I do not propose to continue longer, Mr. Speaker, I am disappointed that nothing has been done in the direction in which I should like to see the government go. This is not a Liberal budget. As I listened to the hon. member for York South, who is nominally a Conservative, I thought this was a conservative budget and that it was very difficult indeed for a member of the Conservative party to criticize it. What we need to-day are progressive economic, social and financial measures, but we are not getting them. That is why all across this country at the present time there is a rising tide of discontent. We find it everywhere. Criticisms are being levelled against this parliament; criticisms that in the main I think are unfair are borne out to some extent by this parliament itself. To-day, for example, we have the budget debate; but while the hon. member for York South was speaking this afternoon I counted at one time only twenty government supporters in their seats, and there were not very many more on the opposition benches. That goes to show that parliament is apathetic, and I believe hon. members of this parliament are disillusioned. The time has come, I say, when in the Dominion of Canada we need a forward-looking policy for the people of this country, and the government is giving neither the policy nor the leadership necessary to bring about the formation of it.
