I should like to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) on his very fine speech and on the return to health which enabled him to make it. But, having done so, I must cease to congratulate him.
The minister closed his remarks with a fine appeal for Canadian unity, for facing up to realities and setting out to change the conditions which are making us lack national esprit de corps and all that. I notice, Mr. Speaker, that in these days members of the cabinet are prone to wind up almost every public utterance with some appeal for Canadian unity. This astounds me, because no other cabinet in the history of Canada has done more to destroy Canadian unity than this cabinet. I do not remember reading about any former cabinet ministers in the history of Canada who seemed more completely unable to see what was causing disunity than hon. gentlemen who now occupy the government benches. I had planned to vent my indignation against them to some extent; I was going to point out to them some of the things which right under their very noses are destroying western Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What alternative does the hon. member suggest to promote unity?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If my right hon. friend will bring up the question after I have finished my speech, I shall have more time to deal with it. A great many things have developed through the years which are destroying the morale and strength of western Canada. I am not blaming this government for it, but do blame the government for doing nothing to improve matters to any great extent.
I was going to point out that western Canada is a primary producing area; consequently it is prone to fall into debt to a secondary producing area. In any well-planned economy there should be a conscious effort to extend favours to the primary producers so as to help them to overcome the handicap under which they are placed by simply being primary pro-

ducers. I do not intend to enlarge upon the matter to any considerable extent. I was going to point out, further, that according to the testimony given by Doctor Jacob Viner last year in Ottawa, the tariff policies of this government are costing the three prairie provinces $47,000,000 a year for the privilege of being in this nation.
I was going to point out further the absolute abominations which exist with respect to our transportation policies. I shall mention two or three, and then pass on, because before I close I must deal with some of the observations of the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lawson). There exists a set of circumstances touching our national transportation policies as a result of which, we have such glaring inequalities as the following: It costs 75 cents per hundredweight to ship barbed wire to Vancouver, whereas to ship it to Edmonton costs $1.98 per hundredweight, making the Edmonton rate 164 per cent of the Vancouver rate. Alberta needs barbed wire.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And good high fences, too.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If the hon. member speaks out again, the first thing he knows I will be saying something he will not forget. The rate to Vancouver on iron and steel bars is 65 cents per hundredweight, and $1.79 to Edmonton; on shoes to Vancouver it is $2 per hundredweight and $3.03 to Edmonton; on twine to Vancouver it is $1.30 and to Edmonton $2,334. I could go through a list of over a hundred items, every one of which would be just as glaring as the ones I have set out. We have allowed to develop in this country a set of unfair conditions like that, and we wonder why the provinces which are being bled to death are suffering. Apparently we do not have sense enough to take any measures to prevent the pressure of those burdensome realities upon the western provinces. And then we stand up and talk about unity!
There was another point I was going to develop, but which I shall only refer to in passing. It is this, that since 1914, by such measures as the eight per cent sales tax, the federal government has been invading the taxation field of the provinces, as a result of which it is drawing from within the boundaries of those provinces the very money that the provinces need in order to stand the pressure being placed upon them as a result of relief, increased social services and that sort of thing. And still the federal government, under the Conservative administration which has ceased to be and under the Liberal administration we now have, has proposed a loan council to force the provinces into such a position

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore
that they simply cannot move. I was going to deal at length with this point and perhaps with several others-because I have mentioned only four out of eight-but some observations of the hon. member who spoke for the official opposition I shall have to attend to.
The hon. gentleman pointed out that it was necessary to increase the durable goods in a country, and placed on record statistics from which he drew a conclusion which I should think any well-informed high school graduate would not seriously have drawn. However I shall not attempt to reflect upon his judgment; we will suppose he was just playing politics.
I ask this question: How are you going to increase the durable goods in a country when you cannot find markets in that country for the production of the durable goods which are already there? To put a concrete case: Let us suppose we are talking about coal mining machinery. How are you possibly going to increase the money invested in coal mining machinery when you cannot find a market for the coal which the present machinery can readily produce? That question calls only for the application of plain economics-the simplest A B C's of economics. One would think social crediters would not have to come down here to Ottawa to deliver a lecture to one of the prominent members of the Conservative party in respect to a matter such as this. It ought to be perfectly clear to anybody who has studied economics. The only way in the wrorld in which you will get more money invested in factories, durable goods and capital equipment in Canada is to increase the markets available for the product of the equipment already here.
The question confronting us is purely one of how to increase markets. There are only two places to find markets, namely, outside and inside the country. The Liberal government has devoted its effort to exploiting the possibility of obtaining external markets. Their aim is a laudable one, but the difficulty is that they run into certain realities which are extremely painful and which I believe tend to destroy the result of all their work.
For example, in order to sell New Zealand and Australian automobiles, rubber goods, wood pulp and the like, governments-not this one particularly-have reduced the duty on Australian and New Zealand butter and mutton and have allowed those products to come into a country which already is able to produce far more of those commodities than it can use. How can you improve economic conditions in a country by policies of this kind it passes any kind of simple common sense to see. But that has been done and is being
done. I believe the Liberal administration will discover that the results of these treaties, upon which it has congratulated itself, will be practically nullified or brought to a dead level by such factors as those I have indicated.
What can we do about internal markets? The social credit philosophy and the Conservative philosophy agree in this respect, that you must increase purchasing power in your country. Apparently the Conservatives have the idea that you can do that by raising the tariff wall high enough. The Social Crediters say that you will never do it by raising the tariff wall, that there is a deficiency of purchasing power which it is utterly impossible to overcome even though you keep every dollar's worth of goods from outside from coming into the country. The hon. member pointed out that he did not agree with his social credit friends. I rather think that is to the credit of those social credit friends. If he was no clearer in his reasoning than he was on the point I mentioned a few moments ago, it certainly would be no credit for the social credit people to be in conformity with him.
I am going to refer to a set of figures which I brought to the attention of the house once before, and which may be found in a book called The Income of the United States. These figures, which will be found on pages 242 to 248, deal with the economy of the United States in 1918. It is pointed out that 60 billion dollars' worth of consumable goods were produced in the United States in that year, that is, goods such as milk, cream, butter, shoes, clothes, and so on. But in that year only 45 billion dollars' worth of money was paid out to the people by every means that could be named-that is, by wages, salaries, dividends, bonuses, and the like. The problem which confronted the United States in 1918 was how to find the purchasing power to buy that extra 15 billion dollars' worth of goods.
The ordinary economist will say that the velocity of circulation should take care of that, but in saying so the ordinary economist makes the greatest mistake of his life. No matter how you juggle things around you cannot make 45 billion dollars' worth of purchasing power buy 60 billion dollars' worth of goods. The big question is how you are going to overcome that. Let us get back to the question raised by the hon. member with regard to durable goods. If you were living in a country where 60 billion dollars' worth of goods were being produced and the people could buy only 45 billion dollars' worth of those goods, what

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore
would be the use of erecting factories to fabricate more goods? If you lived in such a country, would you go into the production of coal when there already was more coal in the country than could be sold? Would you be willing to spend any money to develop a shoe factory when there was already being produced more shoes than the people could buy? I could go down the whole list of commodities. We should ask ourselves with respect to how many diiferent commodities do we produce more in Canada than the people can buy. I think hon. members would be amazed to find out how many there are. I do not say we are producing more than the people could buy if we gave them the necessary purchasing power, but we are producing more than they can buy with the income at present at their disposal.
When hon. members on both sides of the house finish thinking through that problem they will be ready for social credit. Of course they are not ready now, because it is quite clear that they have not thought through the problem. The problem is there, however, and by and by even they will see, although they cannot see to-day.
A good deal of more or less superior, patronizing tolerance and indulgence is shown by certain wise men in parliament to-day toward social credit because we talk about putting money into the hands of the people. The men who assume that attitude are quite unconscious of the type of men with whom they are colliding when they take a more or less scornful attitude toward this idea of putting purchasing power into the hands of the consumer.
As an example, I should like to quote Doctor Leonard Alston, lecturer in economics at Cambridge university. I should like to quote from page 77 of his book entitled The Functions of Money, published by the Macmillan Company in 1932. I am going to ask hon. members to indulge me while I read from this publication. Apparently there is no use in my talking, but if I put on Hansard the words of a man who at least deserves respect, whether or not they agree with them, hon. members may read those words and reflect. Here is what he says:
The banks are accustomed, when expanding monetary supplies, to pump them in at the producers' end; and producers and bankers together may well make the gravest mistakes as to the proportions in which the rest of us will want to buy cotton goods or coal, houses or cars, cinema tickets or beer. . . . And so the producers, however fully informed of the state of affairs at the moment, may come to be disappointed in the end, with the natural, and probably inevitable, result that we have gluts and shortages (of types of labour and of plant) simultaneously present all over the field.
rMr. Blackmore.]
I am closing the quotation there. That is an admirable picture of the condition that exists to-day all over Canada and the United States because we have chosen to inject money through production. This is to be found on page 78:
Would it, then, be possible to neglect the producers and pour the new money freely into the hands of the consumers-that is to say, into the hands of all of us (seeing that consumers are not a class, but the whole community under another name) ? If all possible buyers were to be given the extra money, their demands on the traders should ensure . . . that all the things they desire would be produced in almost the right proportions, and we should no longer be faced with the recurrent problems of overproduction of this and relative underproduction of that . . . leaving hands stranded high and dry, along with their unemployed machinery, unable to buy their customary share of the textiles and coal and cinema performances that other wrorkers would have been eager to supply if satisfactory buyers could have been found, but owing to the absence of these buyers were constrained to stop supplying and become unemployed themselves.
From the coldly intellectual point of view there would seem to be a great deal to be said in favour of this way of handling the problem. We should all be getting a larger share of the things we desire, and we should all be getting a larger demand for our own services, so that under-employment would be confined to those, in the specially overpopulated industries, who were specially immobile and unadaptable for other work ... it would work admirably, no doubt, if all of us were unemotionally intelligent and realized clearly what was happening.
I submit that here is a man who surely is worthy of some respect, and his statement supports perfectly the social credit contention. Of course the hon. member for York South does not agree with him. Naturally he is a greater economist than this man. I have here another quotation which I think almost everyone in this house should give ear to. I intend to quote from a book entitled Prices and Production, written by Friedrich A. von Hayek, lecturer in economics, university of Vienna, and director of the Austrian statistical institute. I quote from page 23 as follows:
... it is perfectly clear that, in order that the supply of and demand for real capital be equalized, the banks must not lend more or less than has been deposited with them as savings. And this means naturally that they must never change the amount of their circulation. At the same time it is no less clear that, in order that the price level remain unchanged, the amount of money in circulation must change as the volume of production increases or decreases.
Now I am going to ask this question: If already in a country there is more coal ready to be produced than the people can use, and consequently the banks can no longer lend money and the owners of money can no

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore
longer invest it in the production of coal, how-will the coal industry be able to put into people's hands any money with which to buy coal other than that money which they would ordinarily get through their labour? It is a well known fact that to-day modern machinery is replacing labour, and therefore decreasing the amount of money which is going into the hands of labour. The result is that unquestionably the amount of purchasing power available to buy coal is decreasing progressively. That is characteristic of the age we live in, this age of plenty, this age of machinery. It has a bearing on the quotation.
I read again from page 11:
Everything depends on where the additional money is injected into circulation, and the effects may be quite opposite according as the additional money comes first into the hands of traders and manufacturers or directly into the hands of salaried persons employed by the state.
By that of course he means consumers.
We hear the statement often made these days that the banks will not lend any more money to industry. We hear again that the banks are full of money. We had the president of the Bank of Canada express in committee a few days ago the idea that the banks can do no more through monetary policy. He is perhaps correct. The banks probably can do no more through monetary policy so long as they continue to think they can put money into circulation only by lending it for production. But if they begin to put it into circulation as consuming money, then something certainly can be done by monetary policy.
The next question that arises is: Will new money that is paid out to people cause inflation? It needs to be borne in mind that so long as you have unemployed men and unemployed resources you cannot have inflation. Unemployment of both men and resources means deflation. Once that fact is fixed in our minds we can begin to do effective thinking on this question of increasing money and its effect on inflation.
I am going to give a quotation or two from an eminent authority across the line, Senator Owen, who testified before a committee of the United States senate in the course of a discussion on farm commodity prices, on June 9, 1937. Here is the first quotation that has a bearing on the question under discussion:
Inflation does not occur until maximum employment and production is achieved. If it should occur the volume of money could be immediately reduced by selling bonds, by sales tax and other taxes and retiring such excess money from circulation.
It is quite clear what he means. I read another passage from his evidence:
And the minute you go beyond the point where you employ all the labour in this country at fair wages for the turnover of their products and services to the country-whenever you go beyond that requirement you are inflating, and when you are down below the normal of full employment, you cannot inflate.
Statements like that appear to be somewhat at variance with the ideas ordinarily expressed by men like the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), the president of the Bank of Canada and other financial authorities in this country. The question arises, who is right? Well, I am wagering that Senator Owen is right, and the next generation will prove it. Here is another quotation from Senator Owen before the same committee:
It is a matter of supreme importance to keep in mind, and at all times to remember, that when you double production it has a tendency to decrease the market price of commodities and thereby to offset the rise in the price of commodities which would take place as a result of expanding the money supply. So long as the expansion of the money supply results in the expansion of employment and increased production of commodities, the one offsets the other. The commodity index is diminished hy the increase of commodities unless the money supply increases at the same time. Increasing the money supply will absorb the unemployed until maximum production is achieved. Maximum production and the absorption in private industry should be our objective.

They are just fooling.
The Budget-Mr. Blackmore

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, just fooling.
The next question is, how is the money to go out into circulation? There has been a good deal of discussion on that ipoint. The Minister of Finance and a great many of his supporters have apparently assumed that the social credit people have advocated running the printing presses. That is not so. The credit should be issued through the banks. Senator Owen puts it rather well. If the committee will allow me to give one more quotation from him, then I think they will have something which they can understand quite well. Senator Owen says:
I think it would be a better plan to pay it out by cheque against a direct credit placed with the reserve banks. It would not be paid out in currency, but could be converted into currency if desired.
In a general way that well expresses the social credit idea. The technique by which that is to be done we must leave to the banks to work out; but it can be done.
It is commonly said, as I mentioned a few moments ago, that nothing more can be done by monetary policy. Those in this country who take that standi are directly at variance with at least one eminent authority from Great Britain. This man is William A. Shaw, editor of the Calendar of Treasury Records. The quotation I am giving is from a book entitled The Principles of Currency, Credit and Exchange, by William A. Shaw and Alfred Wigglesworth, published in 1934. Here is what they say:
In enunciating for the banks the simple principle which must guide them in this task of controlling an upward or prosperity phase, it is not difficult to lay down a rough-and-ready datum line from which to start. That line is simply such a level of prosperity as will keep the whole of our economic system functioning healthily, and will provide suitable sustenance to every man, woman and child in the land, and suitable employment to every employable person: a level which will yield a fair return to capital and make a fair provision for the development of social and other services which have become so important a factor in our national life. We think that such a datum level can be defined, not as a theorem, but as a matter of practical common sense.
There is what that eminent authority thinks. When men maintain, that nothing more can be done by monetary policy they are certainly in direct contradiction to that authority.
It is argued at the present time that if more money is put into the hands of the people it will hurt somebody, but no effort is made to explain how that will come about. I have, on three or four occasions, noticed in the press reports to that effect. Let me put before the house this simple situation. Suppose that Henry Ford were to move to Can-

ada and were to bring with him $1,000,000,000,
Suppose he settled in western Canada and proceeded to spend that $1,000,000,000. Is there anyone in this house who would suggest that this would hurt anyone in Canada? It sounds nonsensical, does it not? Many times we have heard people say what a good thing it would be to have capital come into the country, and yet the moment it is proposed that we should print $100,000,000 of bills and pay a bonus to the farmers in the west therewith, w,e are told that it would hurt someone. Well, it remains for the people who take that stand to show that the printing of $100,000,000 of Canadian bills would have a different effect from the bringing into, this country of, say $100,000,000 by a Henry Ford or anybody else. Suppose that instead of $100,000,000 we had one billion. Personally I think that would be too much at the present time, although to think that Canada could not be made to absorb one billion dollars is a piece of nonsense, considering the number of people who could go. to work, and the extent of our resources. But suppose one billion dollars were spent all over Canada, distributed per capita throughout, the country and spent in the large cities. How in the world can anyone consistently and logically reason that the expenditure of this money would hurt anybody?
I think I have said enough at present, but I am going to lay this down as a solemn principle and be laughed at again. I say that you will never be able to change conditions in this country; you will never be able to solve the unemployment problem; you will never be able to diminish taxation; you will never be able consistently to balance your budget or pay off the debt until you change the system under which we are working. I do not hesitate to leave that statement on Hansard and let future generations declare whether I am right or wrong. And all that is happening throughout the world at the present time, all that is happening in every country, I call as evidence in support of my contention.
We have reached the point where the machinery and technical skill that we possess can create goo'ds in greater abundance than the income of the people will permit them to buy, and until we supplement the buying power of the people to enable their purchasing power to equal the value of the goods produced, we shall go on doing absurd things, as pointed out by the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). speechtext:
Mr. MAXIME RAYMOND (Beauharnois-Laprairie) moved the second reading of Bill No. 31, to amend the Companies Act. 1934.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the object of the bill of which I now move second reading is to amend the Companies Act, 1934, to give the Secretary of State the means of exercising adequate supervision over the operations and conduct of companies incorporated under this act, and especially to enable him to ascertain that companies enjoying the protection of the customs tariff are not guilty of abuse and are not exercising the powers and privileges granted to them to the detriment of the public and the workers.
I was prompted to introduce this bill by the crying abuses revealed by the royal commission on the textile industry which was presided over by Hon. Mr. Justice Turgeon, abuses intolerable in a well-organized society, which have deeply stirred public opinion and which call for drastic repressive action by parliament.
Although the principle of the bill does not apply to any one industry I shall limit my remarks to the industry which was the cause
of the investigation just mentioned.
On January 15, 1936, Mr. Blair Gordon, managing director of the Dominion Textile Company, disgruntled at the refusal of the
Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) to agree to his request that a tariff equivalent to a tax of 494J per cent be maintained on Japanese goods, undertook on his sole responsibility to suspend operations at the Sherbrooke mill and notified the federal authorities that the refusal of the Minister of Finance would throw 500 to 600 textile workers out of employment. As a matter of fact, the following notice was issued the next day:
This mill will close on Friday, January 17, and will remain closed indefinitely.
(Signed) G. B. Gordon,
Managing Director.
Mr. Gordon immediately informed the public, through the medium of the press, that on account of Japanese competition with respect to certain types of artificial silk the mill had to be closed, and would remain closed as long as a possibility of manufacturing goods that would sell could not be foreseen. And this incident took place in the middle of the winter and in the midst of general unemployment.
I do not even attempt to qualify such a process of intimidation on the part of the managing director of an industry which thrives on privileges granted by parliament. The government's answer was the appointment of a royal commission presided over by the Hon. Mr. Justice Turgeon, with power to inquire "with respect to all matters surrounding the operations and conduct of the textile industry." The order in council was passed on January 27. Two days later the Sherbrooke mill was reopened, and it has been in continuous operation ever since. Mr. Gordon's bluff had been called. But here we have an idea of the inhuman measures that this young dictator can resort to in an attempt to intimidate the government and achieve his purpose, and without any regard for the distress of the workers.
A brief analysis of the facts revealed by the evidence adduced before the commission shows the odiousness of his conduct. In March, 1935, Japan had complained of the restrictions placed on the imports of Japanese goods to Canada. Ensuing negotiations had been unsuccessful, and following mutual reprisals the duties were again raised, to such an extent that they constitute an almost prohibitive barrier between Canada and Japan.
Since August, 1935, customs and excise duties on a bolt of artificial silk worth $43.60 amounted to $215.62, this last amount corresponding to a tax of 494i per cent.
Under an agreement concluded in November, 1935, to take effect on January 1, 1936, the duties were substantially reduced. By virtue of this agreement the customs and

Companies Act-Mr. Raymond
excise duties on that same bolt of artificial silk worth S43.60 were only $83.42, an amount equivalent to a tax of 191i per cent.
In spite of this reduction in the customs duties claimed to bring about the ruination of Mr. Gordon's industry, the Sherbrooke mill, which was reopened two days after the passage of the order in council appointing the royal commission, on January 29, 1936, has been in continuous operation ever since. On December 7, 1936, wages at the mill were raised to a maximum of 7 per cent. This raise was accompanied by the following announcement:
General improvement of our operations as shown by the number of orders on hand at the present time is the main reason for this increase, of salaries.
The annual report on the operations of the company for the year ending March 31, 1937, contained the following paragraph:
We have been fortunate in securing a good volume of business over the past twelve months or so, despite further reductions in the tariff during the interval.
The royal commissioner was severe in his condemnation of the unjustifiable attitude taken by Mr. Gordon, and in his reference to the duties of tariff protected industry he added:
Without this tariff the consumer would be at liberty to buy his requirements in whatever market he chooses, and at free trade prices.
. . . The community has consented, through parliament, to tax itself for the benefit of an industry which turns out a product which everybody must use, and which, in a large measure, is not indigenous to Canada. . . . The community, therefore, is entitled to some substantial benefit from such an industry in return for the great privilege bestowed on it.
And his report concludes as follows:
In the case of a manufacturer operating under a protective tariff . . . there is surely an implied undertaking on the part of the manufacturer, so long as he continues to enjoy the advantage of the tariff, to refrain from throwing workmen out of employment, especially in times of distress, without reasonable justification or excuse.
This is an outline of the situation obtaining at the Sherbrooke mill. The order in council, however, went much farther. The commissioner was ordered to secure complete information with respect to the textile industry, with a view of ascertaining, among other things, whether it actually discharged its obligations to its employees and the public.
Let us examine the operations and conduct of some of the textile companies in the light of the revelations made in the course of the inquiry, and let us see how those companies understood their duties.
It was claimed by the leaders of the textile industry, as the commissioner pointed out in

his report, that their industry could not subsist without the protection of a customs tariff. The customs tariff is a tax imposed on the consumer by the state for the benefit of certain industries. Such a tax constitutes a very heavy burden for the workers themselves. The customs tariff compels the consumer to pay for an article manufactured in Canada a much higher price than if that same article were purchased in the open market.
Why, then, should the state be willing to impose a special tax on the consumer for the benefit of the textile industry? Why should the consumer be compelled to pay more for a product made in Canada? Surely it is not to enable some financiers to accumulate colossal fortunes at the expense of the public and the workers. It is because the state expects and has the right to expect, manufacturing companies enjoying special privileges for which the public pays the shot, to give the workers steady employment and pay them fair wages that will enable them to live and bring up their families decently. It must be kept in mind that the profits actually made by an industry such as the textile industry, claiming that its very existence depends on tariff protection, are derived from this tax placed on the consumer, and also from tax exemptions and bonuses granted by municipal corporations.
It is, therefore, the duty of every company thus protected by a customs tariff to give regular employment to the largest possible. number of workers and to pay them a living wage. Further, wages paid by an industry thus protected, should be given priority over the allotment of dividends, and particularly over dividends paid on watered stock.
Let us take the case of The Montreal Cottons Ltd. In 1880, the capital invested in that company was $385,000. That same year, the company paid a dividend of eleven per cent to its shareholders. The following year, profits were so high that an amount of $110,000 was paid to the shareholders in the form of a share bonus, at the same time as a 20 per cent dividend was declared. Between 1881 and 1911, The Montreal Cottons Ltd. paid its shareholders, on both actually paid and watered capital stock, dividends ranging from 6 per cent to 20 per cent. These were paid at a time when the company enjoyed tax exemptions and secured a bonus of $50,000 from the city of Valleyfield, the seat of its operations.
In 1911, its capital had swelled to $3,000,000. Notwithstanding the generous dividends paid, the accumulated profits were so large that a

Companies Act-Mr. Raymond
stock bonus amounting to $3,000,000 was paid to the shareholders. Since 1911, the company has continued to pay dividends on a capital of 36,000,000, although the total investment does not exceed $2,890,000.
In short, besides the substantial dividends paid on the capital actually invested, The Montreal Cottons Ltd. has paid, with the consumers' money-thanks to tariff protection- with the exemption from municipal taxes, with the money that should have been paid in wages to the worker, and with the money obtained in the form of bonuses, dividends approximating $4,000,000 on watered stock. This watered stock is now carried on the books at a value of $5,000,000. This represents but a portion of the profits, 'because some accumulated profits were not distributed.
What was the share of the workers compared with that received by the shareholders who benefited from tariff adv ,ntages granted by parliament to the textile industry? The workers were treated like slaves. Their average annual wage does not exceed $300. In Valley-field, where the mill is located, the worker is constantly made to feel that he owes his very existence to the company. Alas, what an existence! The man who sweats in the mill from six o'clock at night until seven o'clock the next morning for a measly pay of $1.08, upon which he has to support four children besides his wife, does not live; he barely keeps body and soul together. I could mention dozens of cases of which I have conclusive evidence, to show that the wages received for two weeks' work range from $6 to $20. When the workers go to get their meagre wages twice a month they are kept waiting for hours, in the rain or in the cold, in a yard without any shelter, and their pay is handed to them in the form of a small ticket., about the size of a postage stamp, on which appears the amount paid and the date of payment. They have no way of knowing the terms of their employment, whether they work by the hour or by the piece, or whether what they receive is the pay they are actually entitled to.
Not a day goes by that I do not receive complaints from these fine workers, whose only wish is to make an honest living. Not long ago I received a letter from one of them asking me to find him another job. This man stated that he had been working at the Montreal Cottons Ltd. mill for the last six years and had never received more than $12 for two weeks' work, with eight children to support. As one may well suspect, the health of the 71492-212
children is often impaired as a result of the unjust poverty in which these people are compelled to live.
Under the threat of dismissal young women are compelled to request the minimum wages commission to permit them to work at rates lower than those set by the commission.
That is the worker's share. Yet the president of the company, in his annual report of March 15, 1938, had the impudence to refer to the general prosperity of the employees and to hint at a reduction in wages in order to bring down the cost of production.
When it is seeking to obtain a tax exemption, the company threatens the citizens that it will close down its mill unless the by-law granting the exemption is passed. When the workers complain, they are told that the reason why a larger number are not given employment and wages are not higher is that the customs tariff is too low.
Since the workers organized a trade union they have had to live in the shadow of unrelenting spying. In his evidence given before the commission the general manager stated that he would not deal with that organization. He said:
We are the people running the mills and we know what we have to do.
In summarizing the situation, it may be said that at Valleyfield The Montreal Cottons Ltd., because of the privileges granted by parliament and without which it claims it cannot exist, constitutes a "state within a state." On the other hand, the workers are rightly asking for adequate measures of protection.
The number of employees has had a tendency to diminish. The machine is displacing the worker, and the latter is being assigned a greater number of looms to operate. In 1931 and 1932, the company purchased machinery to an amount of $1,500,000. Production increases for the benefit of the shareholders and to the detriment of the weaver. For instance, exhibits filed by the company at the inquiry showed that in 1903 the total sales amounted to $2,384,416, as against $5,-
189,000	in 1935, with 246 fewer workers being employed. The production had more than doubled, yet the number of workers employed had been reduced by a few hundreds. If we compare 1935 with 1929, we find that the average number of workers employed decreased by 898; the number of weavers employed decreased by 50 per cent, and the total wages paid to them also decreased by 50 per cent. This is a brief summary of the situation with respect to The Montreal Cottons Ltd.

Companies Act-Mr. Raymond
When we consider the Dominion Textile Company, we are faced with still more outrageous conditions. We have there the most cynical example of abuses committed by a certain type of financiers who are constantly asking parliament for new privileges in order better to exploit the public and the worker, while posing as benefactors of humanity.
The Dominion Textile Company was incorporated in 1905. Mr. Howson, accountant to the royal commission, computed that on an initial investment of $500,000 in 1905, the shareholders, among whom were Sir Charles Gordon and Sir Herbert Holt, had received between 1905 and 1936 a sum of $14,837,000 in dividends, and in addition, the shares had a value of $14,671,105. Those shareholders are still receiving dividends at the rate of 150 per cent on their original investment.
This represents but a small fraction of the profits made by the company, Exhibits filed before the commission showed that the Dominion Textile Company, in addition to the dividends allotted, is accumulating huge profits from year to year, some of which appear on the balance sheet under various heads, while others are concealed. The commission's counsel claims that, since 1926, in addition to declared profits, the company would have made $1,000,000 yearly which does not appear on the balance sheet.
Do hon. members think for one moment that the company is satisfied with those profits? Oh, no! Let me quote a statement made by the president in his annual report in May, 1922, when he was receiving dividends at the rate of 120 per cent on his investment of 1905, and shortly after he had caused a bonus of $35,000 to be voted to him:
I really cannot see myself why the finance minister should bleed Canadian industry for the benefit of Great Britain or any other country.
Every year this same lament, that the tariff is too low and that profits are small and barely allow for a modest return to the shareholders, is heard from the president.
The company's counsel stated before the commission:
The earnings of the company have been and are entirely inadequate, and do not represent a fair yield upon the value of the investment.
How do the wages paid to the workers compare with the shareholders' profits, and what advantages have the workers derived from the privileges granted to the textile industry?
Information published by the company itself shows that between 1905 and 1914, the average annual wages paid to the workers amounted to between $266 and $291-and this while

the shareholders were receiving dividends of 50 per cent and 60 per cent on their investment.
In his brief to the commission, the company's counsel dared to state:
The company has provided continuous employment, at rates of wages reasonable.
In September, 1930, the employers asked for an increase in the tariff-more privileges, in other words-promising that they would employ a larger number of workers. The manufacturers have taken advantage of the increased protection to augment their production, not by increasing the number of employees but by purchasing machinery of foreign origin, which has displaced the workers. Between 1926 and 1936, the textile industry imported machinery to the value of $38,000,000 -production was increased, but labour was reduced-and in 1933, while the Dominion Textile was paying dividends at the rate of 150 per cent on the 1905 investment, the wages of its employees were reduced by 10 per cent to 20 per cent. This is the way in which the company passes on to the workers the favours it obtained from parliament in 1930 and 1931.
The intention of parliament, as it was stated by Mr. Bennett at the time, was "to ensure additional employment to a larger number of men and women in Canada."
Mr. Whitehead, managing-director of the Wafoasso Cotton Company Limited, admitted that the labour percentage in a manufactured product had decreased from 32 per cent in 1928 to 20 per cent in 1935; that to manufacture sixteen million yards of cloth in 1928 he had employed 2,450 workers, with total wages of $1,500,000, whereas in 1935, to manufacture thirty-seven million yards of cloth, he had employed only 1,858 workers, with total wages of $971,000. The company's production was more than double, but its employees have been reduced in number by 25 per cent and their wages by 33 per cent.
What are the advantages accruing to the workers? The inquiry revealed that the manufacturers had but one thing in mind: to secure an ever-increasing tariff, to increase their production by substituting machinery for workers, and to reduce wages-and all in order to increase their profits. To achieve their purpose, all methods of intimidation were considered fair. Was it with the intention of serving such a purpose that parliament granted to the textile industry the privilege of taxing the consumer?

Companies Act-Mr. Raymond
The employers are prosperous while their employees live in misery.
Parliament is laughed at; the consumer is laughed at; and the worker is laughed at!
Each year, in his report, the president of the Dominion Textile Company repeats that the protection granted to the industry is inadequate to ensure a fair return to the shareholders, and that the workers are well paid and well treated. On occasions he has even stated that salaries and wages were too high. And all this took place while the president was cashing in on dividends at the rate of 150 per cent on his initial investment, while he was causing a $35,000 bonus to be voted to him, as in 1921, and while he was receiving an annual salary of $20,000 to $25,000 as president. But during all this time he was paying starvation wages to his workers.
Take a glance at the advertisements inserted at great cost by the company-and mind you, it is the consumer who pays for them-in the newspapers, and look at the pamphlets it publishes, not to advertise its products but to publicize its good deeds. Well, Mr. Speaker, if it is the intention of the company to publicize its so-called generosity, the bill now before us should help it to achieve its purpose.
This is a picture in miniature of the operations and conduct of companies which have enjoyed special privileges, representing heavy charges upon the consumer, and which have, in return, persistently refused to acknowledge their responsibilities to parliament, to the public and to the workers.
The inquiry has revealed the prosperous condition of the shareholders, in contrast to the physical and mental distress of the workers, in an industry taxing consumers and workers alike. It would be a challenge to common sense to imagine that this denial of common justice was meant to be perpetrated by virtue of powers and special privileges granted by parliament. Drastic legislation is imperative to curb the activities of those ogres of finance and industry who, with the cynicism of gangsters, profit by the misery of thousands of workers. Parliament is supreme; within its jurisdiction it has the power and the duty to act. If parliament does not take drastic steps, it will become the accomplice of this exploitation.
Limited companies exist only by the will of the state. Our Companies' Act has already been amended in 1934 in order to protect the investor; it is now time to amend it to protect the public and the workers-workers who are sometimes defenceless, like those at 71492-212$
Valleyfield, who are at the mercy of the cupidity and threats of a powerful company exercising a tyrannical power over them.
In his report, the royal commissioner emphasized, in unmistakable terms, the duties and obligations of an industry enjoying special privileges, and the duties and obligations of the granting authority. The amendments I now propose to the Companies' Act are based on that report, and are intended to put an end to the abuses revealed by the investigation.
In order to dispel any doubt that might exist in the minds of members of this house, I point out that section 121, which the bill proposes to amend, does not apply to loan companies, trust companies, railway companies, insurance companies, penny banks or to the chartered banks. Further, some of the proposed amendments apply only to tariff-protected companies. Section 83a applies only to public companies incorporated by letters patent issued by the Secretary of State, and protected by the tariff.
To justify these amendments I cannot do better than to quote certain passages in the royal commissioner's report. At page 117 he says:
It is the fact that the Canadian textile indus-enjoys and has enjoyed for many years, the advantages of a protective tariff, which makes it accountable to the community for the condition of its affairs. The community, having accepted the sacrifice of the tax imposed upon it for the industry's benefit, has the consequent right to know what is going on under the regime thereby created, presumably in the interest of the nation. ...
[DOT]	.	. it is in my opinion, equally important,
looking to the future, that the affairs of each member of the industry should be so regulated as to make information of this character available, from time to .time, and at fairly frequent intervals, to all concerned.
And on page 127:
Having in mind both the investor and the consumer of manufactured goods-especially of tariff-protected manufactured goods-I suggest that ithe question of the efficient, comprehensive supervision of these company incorporations is well worth the attention, and possibly the cooperation, of both dominion and provincial authorities.
"^°Pinion Parliament which provides the tariff has the right, I may venture, I think, to say the duty, to see to it that true facts are made known, as often as necessary and practicable, concerning, among other things, the profits made by .those who operate under the protection of the tariff.
Further down, the commissioner adds:
Some of the balance sheets shown me under the Companies Act, 1934, are quite deficient.
# It is Quite apparent that the commissioner is of the opinion that it is the right and duty of parliament to inquire into the business*

Companies Act-Mr. Raymond
and particularly into the profits of tariff-protected industries, which, in exchange for such protection, have given their undertaking to the public to account for their operations.
We could thus find out, from the Dominion Textile lavishly advertising that prosperity is everywhere to be found where it operates, how much it pays to each worker in the course of any one year-because, in the end, the worker's main consideration is the total sum required to provide a living for his family during the year. Briefly, we could ascertain whether companies enjoying tariff protection discharge their obligations in return for the privileges they enjoy.
The proposed amendments to section 121 of the Companies' Act would enable us to obtain that information.
Section 83a affords an indispensable protection against the abuses of financiers, by enabling the Secretary of State to control the allotment of dividends. Through manipulations, fictitious capital is created. Shares issued are divided time and time again, in no way corresponding to the investment, and an apparently modest dividend is declared. Thus, in the case of the Dominion Textile, Sir Charles Gordon and Sir Herbert Holt receive actually 150 per cent in dividends on their investment of 1905, although the apparent rate is only five per cent; in 1921 Sir Charles Gordon caused a $35,000 bonus to be voted to him and as president of the company he received an annual salary of between S20.000 and $25,000. This is an illustration of the manner in which the worker is despoiled, for the benefit of shareholders and directors.
A company deriving its profits from a tax on the consumer should be rigidly controlled and strictly limited in its profits, because each dollar of profit is the proceed of a tax.
The following is what Hon. Mr. Justice Turgeon had to say on pages 204 and 205 of his report, with respect to the particular obligations incumbent on the companies enjoying tariff protection:
One might say that the advantage of protection is granted to these companies subject to certain conditions, which parliament should recognize and government should enforce. The first consideration industry puts forward to support its demand for protection is the service it renders and the obligation it assumes respecting employment. . . .
The shareholders' interests may have to give way on occasions to those of the community.
Wages are the essential element of the workers' sustenance and should be given priority over dividends, particularly so when dividends are paid on watered stock or from benefits derived from a tax imposed on the consumer.

I am confident that the control I am now proposing will inspire certain financiers with a somewhat keener sense of humanity and justice in the conduct of their business.
